That would not be so, of course, if the power producing the Forms were a psychic faculty bound to physical matter, needing material instruments and a suitable material receptacle in order to produce them.

But if the power is immaterial (mujarrad)—whether a pure Intelligence or an Intelligence belonging to the world of Images rather than to the world of material things—then it needs neither an instrument nor a receptacle from this material world to produce its Forms and Images.

What the agent does not need in order to be, it likewise does not need in order to bring into being. It is therefore unnecessary to suppose that celestial bodies serve as receptacles in which separated souls cause the Forms they produce to appear. Those Forms subsist through their producer (fāʿil), not through a receiving substrate (qābil).
We may certainly say that the rank of some human souls corresponds to the rank of the Soul governing one Heaven, while the rank of others corresponds to the Soul governing a Heaven above or below it.
Thus Jesus is said to be “in the Fourth Heaven,” the Heaven of the Sun, while Moses is in the Sixth Heaven, the Heaven of Jupiter.
But the Miʿrāj is an ascent through the Heavens of the Soul, the spiritual Heavens of Hūrqalyā—not the feat of an astronaut launched into physical space.

From the very outset, then, the teaching about the world to come depends on the doctrine of Imagination as a purely spiritual faculty. It constitutes, so to speak, the soul's subtle body, with a “physiology” of its own. This teaching also depends on the existence of an autonomous world of Images and imaginal realities, intermediate between the sensible and the intelligible. Without that world, we could explain neither visionary experiences, nor the spiritual meaning of divine Revelations, nor resurrection itself.

The following Glosses will make this clear. “Souls have the power to bring these Images into existence,” declares Suhrawardī. “Whoever has truly understood this theme,” writes Mullā Ṣadrā, “as its true meaning demands, will be able to establish the doctrine of bodily resurrection (maʿād jismānī) without difficulty or strain” (Gloss 614, lithograph, p. 509). This declaration is of the greatest importance: the entire meaning of the human being's destiny after death depends upon it.

Our shaykh goes on to develop the thesis as follows (ibid.). Just as the soul, through its intellectual power of receiving intelligible realities in actuality, is independent of the material physical body, so too is it independent of that body through its imaginative power (quwwat mutakhayyila) and imaginative acts (afʿāl khayālīya).

Thus, when the soul leaves this world, it still has its active Imagination at its service. Through its own essence and this faculty, it can directly perceive concrete things whose existence, as actualized in the soul's knowledge and imagination (wujūduhā'l-ʿilmī wa'l-khayālī), is at the same time their very form of concrete existence. For all the soul's powers are then gathered and concentrated into one faculty, the active Imagination.

The soul is no longer dispersed among the different gateways of the body's five senses, nor distracted by caring for a physical body exposed to all the changes and hardships of the outer world. At last imaginative perception can show its essential superiority over sensory perception.

“All the faculties of the soul have then become as though they were one faculty: the power to give shape and form, to fashion images and figures (taṣwīr and tamthīl). Its imagination has itself become sensory perception; its imaginative sight (baṣar khayālī) is itself its sensible sight (baṣar ḥissī).

“The same holds for hearing, smell, taste, and touch: all these imaginative senses are themselves faculties of sensation. For although the external senses are five in number, each with its own bodily organ, inwardly they all form a single synaisthesis (ḥiss mushtarak, sensus communis), a common sense in which sensation is united.” Here, in outline, is the entire “physiology” of the subtle body and the resurrection body.

It is significant that, at precisely this point, Mullā Ṣadrā turns to Avicenna's doctrine of the Animae caelestes, citing a passage from the Taʿlīqāt. These “celestial Souls” are the Angeli caelestes: angels that carry their respective Heavens in a movement of love toward the Intelligence from which they emanate (the Angeli intellectuales). The celestial Souls have no external senses. They do, however, possess active Imagination in an absolutely pure and perfect state, because in them it is free from the desires and distortions that the senses introduce into Imagination.

The activity of these Animae caelestes helps us understand the activity of human souls—Animae humanae—restored to their proper state, as well as the influence the former may exert on the latter. It also allows us to grasp what was lost when this intermediate angelic hierarchy disappeared from Averroes and Averroism. With that hierarchy, the entire imaginal world vanishes, together with everything bound up with it. The imaginal becomes merely the imaginary. From here we can measure the divergence between the West, where Latin Averroism prevailed, and the East, where Iranian Avicennism endured.

Where the world of the Animae caelestes is present, we find symbolic visionary narratives; where it is absent, there is only fiction. Where that world is present, the Qur'anic verses concerning paradise and hell need be understood neither according to the outward appearance of their literal meaning nor as allegory, but according to their literal spiritual truth. This is achieved through a taʾwīl that is also a taḥqīq: an interpretation that leads the verses back to the plane of being with which they correspond symbolically, and where their true reality can be recognized.

Mullā Ṣadrā therefore gladly calls on a passage from the Taʿlīqāt to confirm his own doctrine. He makes only one reservation: Avicenna should not have identified imaginative perception in the world beyond with what happens during sleep in this life. For even during sleep the imaginative faculty is disturbed by the organic processes occurring in the physical body. It therefore falls far short of the perfection and activity of which it is capable when no other faculty distracts it. Such freedom becomes possible only after death.

“Otherwise, sleep would quite simply be an awakening into the world beyond. This is what is alluded to in the saying of the Commander of the Faithful (or of the Prophet): Human beings are asleep; when they die, they awaken.”

That said, Mullā Ṣadrā is entirely happy, this time, to endorse a long passage from Avicenna's Risālat al-Aḍḥawīya: “The imaginative faculty (quwwat khayālīya) perceives particular realities not as though they were impressed upon it, with the faculty serving as their receptacle, but creatively and actively—as their originator and active producer.” Avicenna thus explains what theologians call the “punishment of the grave” through the grave in its true meaning (qabr ḥaqīqī), which is not the burial ground.

“The soul imagines itself in a form corresponding to its own nature, and it encounters the things promised to it in a manner consistent with the faith it professed. … Hence the Prophet said: The grave is either a garden among the gardens of paradise or a pit among the pits of hell.” We have already seen, however, and will see again, that certain of Avicenna's texts on this subject fall well short of satisfying Mullā Ṣadrā.

Gloss 615 (lithograph, p. 509) emphasizes the reversal that occurs in passing to the world beyond, when imaginative perception regains its precedence over sensory perception. How does the soul make a thing “present to itself”? “Sensory perception follows an encounter with something external to the faculty of sensation. Through Imagination, on the other hand, a Form may come into being through the sheer power of imaginative creation (bi-mujarrad ikhtirāʿ al-mutakhayyila), without being given outside the faculty that perceives it.

“In this world, however, what is perceived through the senses has the greater force. It acts more evidently than what is imagined in producing pleasure or pain. In the world beyond this difference disappears—or rather, the relation is reversed. The things of that world have a stronger mode of being and a more intense power to act, because their unity is more perfect and they are not scattered among material things. They are like the kernel; the things of this lower world are like the bran or the husk.

“The material existence of things in this world is distinct from the mental image we form of them. They therefore do not possess, as mental images, the same solidity that they possess in their concrete existence. In the world beyond, by contrast, the concrete existence of things is identical with their existence as image and perception (wujūd ṣūrī idrākī). The delight they give is therefore all the sweeter, and the suffering they inflict all the more acute.”

In the very long Gloss that follows (Gloss 616, lithograph, p. 513), Mullā Ṣadrā offers a substantial lesson in which, with the clarity of a master who fully understands his own doctrine, he draws together its major principles. To trace the connections among them is to reveal the structure of the whole within which his philosophy of resurrection takes its place, and to show how thoroughly his metaphysics is directed toward the world to come.

Suhrawardī had written: “These Forms”—of the ʿālam al-Mithāl, the mundus imaginalis—“are more perfect than those existing in the world of our sensory experience.” Mullā Ṣadrā begins by citing an unnamed muḥaqqiq, a scholar seeking the truth, who had developed a theory of creative Imagination.

According to that theory, the ultimate difference between this world and the world beyond is one of degree, measured by how completely the imaginative power can make Forms present, effectively and vividly, to the faculty of sight, for example. “There, whatever the active Imagination desires is present to it at once. The soul's desire causes its imaginative representation, and that representation causes its visual perception.”

Interesting as this theory is—and we have quoted only a few lines of it—it does not satisfy Mullā Ṣadrā. “That,” he says, “is our muḥaqqiq's account. Of all that we have read in the words of the learned and of scholars seeking the true meaning (taḥqīq) of maʿād jismānī—the bodily destiny after death, the passage by resurrection from this world to the next—it is the most satisfactory.

“Yet it does not fully succeed. To reach the goal, it must be supplemented and brought to completion. That requires premises that neither this author nor the others adequately possessed. You will soon see that, by way of philosophical-theosophical demonstration, they could neither establish bodily resurrection (maʿād jismānī) nor understand the Forms promised in the world beyond, except by supposing those Forms to be attached to some celestial body or material place of manifestation (maẓhar).

“Otherwise they had to resort to taʾwīl and interpret them as pure intelligible realities.” In other words, without an understanding of the being of the intermediate world—the imaginal world between the sensible and the intelligible, the world of the Animae caelestes—we must either turn these Forms into something material, one way or another, or escape into a rationalizing allegory that dissolves all the richness of the concrete spiritual world.

To escape this dilemma, we need a coherent doctrine, beginning with a metaphysics of being. For our shaykh this is the doctrine he has expounded throughout his writings, and of which we have already given some account. Here he sums it up in eight major theses, himself showing us the order in which his philosophy should be reconsidered.

For every essence, the act of being—its existing—is the concrete existent itself. What a thing is, its quiddity or essence, follows from this act and is united with it in a way entirely its own. (There is not first a ready-made what—a quiddity or essence—which then begins to exist. Rather, a being is what it is in the very act of being: in existing, it brings its essence into actuality. Mullā Ṣadrā is here recalling the fundamental principle of his metaphysics of esse–existere, the act of being and existing, as opposed to a metaphysics that gives priority to essences.)

The act of being has varying degrees of intensity. (As the act of being grows more intense, the essence likewise grows more intense, yet it remains the very same being that undergoes this intensification. Thus all the stages of existence after death belong to the identity of a single act of being that changes and intensifies, and thereby intensifies the essence it brings into actuality. This is the Soul itself.)

Substance, too, can undergo intensification and transformation in its very act of being. The act of existence of a substance (al-wujūd al-jawharī) can grow more intense, more perfect, and can change. These are the metamorphoses (taḥawwul) required for the passage from the physical world into worlds beyond the physical. (Compare the notion of a “transfer in substance” discussed above, and, more generally, Mullā Ṣadrā's characteristic doctrine of movement within substance, or transubstantial movement.)

In every composite being, Form (ṣūrat) is the principle and source of what that being is—of its quiddity or essence. Matter is what bears the potentiality of the composite, the possibility of its act of being. But matter is not a constituent of the composite's essence. Similarly, what philosophers call genera and differentiae are inherent features and accompanying conditions required for a thing's external, material realization. Yet they follow from that which is the principle and source of its essence. If we reflect on Form itself, we discover that it is, in itself and through itself, the principle that gives existence to these features and conditions. Form is what establishes and unifies them as a determinate essence, the subject to which their concepts can be attributed. (This radical transformation of hylomorphism—the doctrine that beings are composed of matter and form—follows from the first thesis, which gives existence precedence over essence. Existence is not added to an already constituted essence; existence establishes and determines the essence, and causes it to vary with its own intensifications.)

It is the soul, or Form, that makes an individual the individual it is. Parts of the body may change, as they do in aging. The present body may even be exchanged for the resurrection body (jism maḥshūr) at the Qiyāmat, the Resurrection. Yet because the soul remains the same soul, the resurrection body is the same as this present body in respect of its Form—which is precisely the soul—even though it is not the same in respect of its matter. Both statements are true: it is the same, and it is not the same. (Here the usual principle that matter is what individuates a being is reversed. Without this reversal, the identity of the resurrection body would be inconceivable, for this body is the fulfillment of the human being's threefold growth as body, soul, and spirit. See Gloss 629 below.)

The imaginative faculty is a substance distinct from and independent of the matter of the physical body (jawhar mujarrad ʿan māddat al-badan). This is something we have already established and demonstrated.

Imaginative Forms (ṣuwar khayālīya) are not stamped or imprinted (munṭabiʿa) upon the Imagination. Rather, they subsist in it as something subsists through its author or active producer (fāʿil), not as something subsists in a passive receptacle (qābil). (Imagination is therefore, in its very nature here, active Imagination.)

Forms whose very nature is to be visible are not imprinted in external matter or in the organ of sight. Visual perception does not consist in a ray issuing from the eye toward an external thing, nor in an impression of that thing upon the eye, nor even in a relation between the soul and a thing outside it. Rather, perception consists in the production of a Form which becomes actual for the soul, emanating from the soul's own world through an illumination bestowed by the Angel who is the Active Intelligence, provided the organ of sight is healthy and all the necessary conditions are present. This illuminative relation (iḍāfa ishrāqīya) joins the soul to a luminous Form of knowledge, not to the dark material Form of the external thing. (This eighth thesis follows from the theory of vision and of knowledge developed by the Illuminationist philosophers, the Ishrāqīyūn.)

We have thus returned to the doctrine of Imagination already outlined in Gloss 614, with all its implications. Mullā Ṣadrā declares here: “In this world there is only one difference between visual perception and imaginative perception. For visual perception the bodily organ and physical matter are constantly required; for imaginative perception they are not.

“But the moment the soul departs from this world and is drawn out of the material body like a sword from its sheath, every trace of mere potentiality, deficiency, and imperfection disappears from the imaginative faculty—I mean the faculty that preserves the sensus communis, the synaisthesis, or unified sense-perception. Then, with its powers of preservation and action brought to perfection, this imaginative faculty itself becomes the source of perfect sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch, without needing a collection of separate organs.
“What is more, the perception of desirable things and the power to bring them into existence become one and the same act, proceeding from one and the same power: the living and imagining Soul.”

Now that our picture of reality has room for the world of the Soul, intermediate between the material world and the purely intelligible world, our shaykh can, in effect, challenge theologians and philosophers alike, represented respectively by Ghazālī and Avicenna.
Mullā Ṣadrā says plainly that Ghazālī and other representatives of established philosophical teaching (ḥikmat rasmīya) have completely missed the point of bodily resurrection (maʿād jismānī).

The deeper reason is their inability to establish the existence of a world of Forms possessing extension or dimension (ṣuwar miqdārīya): Forms that fully exist and can be perceived by the faculty appropriate to them, yet exist neither in material matter nor attached to a maẓhar, a place of manifestation in this world. (As we recalled earlier, it was chiefly Suhrawardī who laid the ontological foundations of the ʿālam al-Mithāl in his Oriental Theosophy. We must understand that achievement in the light of his angelology, which restores the structure of Mazdean cosmology: existence divided into two states, gētīg, material and sensible, and mēnōg, subtle and beyond the senses.) Here Mullā Ṣadrā quotes a long passage from Ghazālī's Kitāb al-Maḍnūn bih.

Ghazālī acknowledges that the Qur'anic descriptions of paradise and hell, as well as the “punishment of the grave,” concern enjoyments and sufferings experienced through sense or Imagination, and therefore presuppose bodily faculties.
Yet, in his view, when soul and body separate, both the sensory faculties and the imaginative faculty disappear. How, then, can those descriptions of life after death retain their meaning?

Ghazālī admits that this is impossible for anyone who does not believe in the resurrection of bodies and who regards the soul's return to a body as absurd. Unfortunately, he gives no explanation of the “resurrection body,” and does not even suggest whether the event might occur on a plane other than the sensible world.

More than that, he does not rule out the possibility that certain celestial bodies—still, therefore, bodies belonging to material physis, or physical nature—might serve as supports for the soul's imaginative activity and sensory faculties after death and at the Resurrection. No one, he says, has ever proved this impossible.

Indeed, in the Kitāb al-Najāt and the Kitāb al-Shifāʾ, Avicenna puts forward this hypothesis, attributing it to “a serious philosopher who does not speak at random.” Ghazālī also admits, however, that Avicenna offered no decisive proof. Still, had Avicenna thought the supposition impossible, he would not have described its author as “a serious philosopher who does not speak at random.”

This is precisely the kind of situation that a thinker like Mullā Ṣadrā finds intolerable: a kind of equivocation, tinged with agnosticism, that seems to leave only the Averroist notion of “double truth” as a way out. It is as though, instead of allowing for several sources of knowledge corresponding to distinct planes of being—planes that differ yet correspond symbolically to one another—we insisted on recognizing only one source of knowledge for one single degree of being. Everything disclosed about other modes or degrees of being would then have to submit to the judgment of that one privileged faculty.

A Shiite thinker whose reflection brings to fruition the esoteric teaching of the holy Imams is not trapped in this dilemma, which sets sheer literalism against rational interpretations or conjectures. We saw above how Mullā Ṣadrā begins the series of propositions leading to his understanding of the mundus imaginalis—a world with its own substantial reality and its own laws—with the defining theses of his metaphysics of being.

We shall have to examine their connections more closely elsewhere. Here our philosopher remarks, not without irony: “At least we can see that in the case of Ghazālī, as in that of the two shaykhs, Fārābī and Avicenna, it is no conjecture at all to observe that their account of the positive reality of bodily resurrection (maʿād jismānī) went no further than admitting that certain celestial bodies in this world—the physical world—might serve as supports for the imaginative presentation of Forms promised after death to souls that are still imperfect.”

But, as Gloss 617 (lithograph, p. 513) sums up, it is unnecessary to suppose that the soul, after death, becomes attached to some celestial body. Here our shaykh refers to his Kitāb al-Mabdaʾ wa'l-Maʿād. To contemplate the Forms that are present to it, the soul needs no external maẓhar, no outside place where they must appear. The soul itself is their maẓhar, their place of manifestation.

Above all, it is an illusion to appeal to the supposed incorruptibility of celestial bodies in order to explain the lasting reality of the Forms of the world beyond. All bodies in our physical world, whether celestial or elemental, are subject at every instant to the same law of change. The preservation and persistence in being attributed to the Forms of the world beyond must instead be traced to the permanence and unfailing actuality of the primordial Beings whose nature is pure activity (Mabādiʾ faʿʿāla): the hierarchies of archangelic Intelligences.

Yet we can understand the hierarchy and interconnection of multiple spiritual universes only if we establish together the existence of the intermediate imaginal world and the transcendence of the imaginative faculty. Two further Glosses will return to these themes.
5. Creative Imagination and Its Role in the Resurrection

“The suspended Forms or Images—that is, images which do not exist within any material substance,” writes Suhrawardi (Eastern Theosophy, § 246), “are not Plato’s Ideas or archetypes (moihol Iflâtûnîya). By their nature, the Platonic archetypes are pure light, whereas some of the suspended Images are dark and others are luminous: the luminous ones belong to the blessed, who delight in them as one delights in contemplating young and beautiful faces; the dark ones belong to the damned, who are tormented by terrifying visions.” This distinction corresponds to the division of the intermediate world between the two cities of Jabalqa and Jabarsa, situated respectively in the east and the west.

We find it described in this way by the mystical philosophers, for example Shams al-Din Lahiji (d. 912/1506–1507). The east is associated with the descent of souls into this world; the west with their ascent from it.

Thus there are souls of light, and souls that have become darkened during their life here. All our authors also distinguish the different levels of the spiritual worlds, as the distinction between Platonic Ideas and the image-forms of the intermediate world requires. Their accounts differ in detail, however, and we cannot examine those differences here.

Broadly speaking, as Gloss 620 reminds us (lithographed edition, pp. 513–514), their various schemes can all be reduced to three worlds: the physical world perceived by the senses (molk); the supersensory world of the Soul (Malakut); and the world of pure Intelligences (Jabarut). Each has its corresponding means of knowledge: the senses, imagination, and intellect.

And, as we have seen, these three correspond in turn to the human triad of body, soul, and spirit, which governs the three stages of human growth from this world into the worlds beyond (see Gloss 629 below). What must be stressed again is that the imaginative faculty must never be confused with what modern people dismiss as “fantasy,” producing nothing but the “imaginary.”

Here imagination is an organ of knowledge and perception (mashâ'ir), as fully as the senses and the intellect are. It is directed toward a world of its own and enables us to know that world. It is a “threshold,” a “window” (rôzana) opening onto another realm. “We have already offered decisive proof,” Mulla Sadra says, “that the intermediate world exists and transcends this world, by demonstrating that the imaginative faculty and the things it perceives are themselves transcendent—that is, immaterial.”

The statement could hardly be clearer. It brings together everything discussed so far and lets us see exactly what is at stake: the philosophy of imaginative perception and the philosophy of resurrection are two sides of the same question. It is significant that, in this very discussion (Gloss 620), Mulla Sadra quotes at length from Ibn Arabi, whose theosophy gives the imagination its fullest possible importance, and whose influence, as we noted earlier, was one of the decisive elements in the thought of the master of Shiraz.

What, exactly, is the nature of this imaginative power, this faculty of forming images, on which our understanding of the true meaning and manner of resurrection depends? And how are we to conceive a world of “suspended” Images, existing without any material support?

Mulla Sadra turns in particular to chapter 63 of Ibn Arabi’s Meccan Spiritual Conquests (Kitâb al-Fotûhât al-Makkîya). The world beyond ordinary experience, which imaginative consciousness alone can perceive, is called an intermediate world: a realm between two worlds, a barzakh.

What does this mean? “The barzakh,” Ibn Arabi writes, “is an ideal boundary between two neighboring things that never encroach upon one another. Take, for example, the boundary between a patch of shadow and an area lit by the sun. The senses cannot find any material division between them; it is the intellect that judges there must be something separating them. That ideal boundary is the barzakh. What the senses perceive is one of the two things—the light or the shadow—not the barzakh itself.

“Yet because the two things are adjacent, they require a barzakh that is neither one nor the other, while holding within itself the possibility of both. This is why, in technical terms, the barzakh is the boundary between what can be known and what cannot, between existence and nonexistence, affirmation and negation, what can be understood and what cannot. It is Imagination, pure and simple. When you perceive and grasp it, you know you are perceiving something that exists, something on which your gaze rests. You know from an unmistakable sign that something is there.
“But what is this thing whose existence you affirm even as you deny it? Imagination is neither existent nor nonexistent, neither known nor unknown, neither affirmed nor denied.”

Ibn Arabi then considers the mirror. Someone looking into it knows that what he sees is not quite his own image (sûrat), yet he cannot deny that it is his image. He also knows that the image is neither inside the mirror nor in the space between himself and the mirror. What, then, is he seeing—this thing that is at once affirmative and negative, existent and nonexistent, known and unknown? The mirror presents a symbolic paradox through which, Ibn Arabi says, “God awakened me to the realization that divine self-manifestations (tajalliyât al-Haqq, theophanies) are subtler still.

“Intellects are so dazzled by them that they ask whether such a manifestation has a ‘whatness,’ an essence, or not. They cannot understand it as sheer nonbeing, because the eye perceives something; but neither can they understand it as being in the absolute sense, because they know it is not an objective thing. It is into a reality of this kind that a person passes during sleep and after death. He sees qualities and attributes as Forms existing in their own right. They speak to him and he speaks to them as though they were bodies (ajsâd) whose reality he cannot doubt.
“The visionary mystic (mokâshif), while awake, sees what the sleeper sees in dreams and what the dead see after death, when they behold in the world beyond the Forms of their own deeds.”

Ibn Arabi then briefly describes the process of taking symbolic form that is essential to imaginative perception. “Although the widest domain of things that can be known belongs to Imagination, even its vast powers cannot receive wholly abstract realities (ma'ânî) as they are in themselves. It sees knowledge, for example, in the form of milk, wine, honey, or a pearl. It sees Islam as a dome or a pillar; the Quran as honey; religion as a chain; God as a human being or as light. It is at once narrow and immense, whereas God is absolutely immense. … Light is the cause of unveiling (kashf) and manifestation (zohûr), for without light the eye perceives nothing.

“God made Imagination a light through which the forms of all things can be perceived. Its light reaches even into nonbeing and gives it form, thereby giving it existence. That is why Imagination deserves the name of light more than anything else in creation that we call luminous.”

This has a crucial consequence for any theory of knowledge. Sense perception does not itself make mistakes: it simply perceives what is given to it. In the same way, imagination, by its own light, perceives what belongs to its domain. Anyone who declares imaginative perception mistaken knows nothing of the conditions under which the light of imagination perceives (idrâk al-nûr al-khayâlî). Likewise, when someone says that sense perception is mistaken, what he is actually judging is something other than perception itself. It is the person making the judgment who errs, not the sense.

Mulla Sadra has a particular purpose in quoting these long passages from Ibn Arabi. He also mentions passages in which Ibn Arabi examines the teachings of the different schools about how human spiritual beings continue to exist and retain their individuality after death. He stops finally at the point where Ibn Arabi introduces the hadith in which the Prophet declares: “Between my tomb and the pulpit from which I preach lies a garden among the gardens of paradise.”

Mulla Sadra then explains: “My purpose in quoting these important passages from Ibn Arabi was to set out the different teachings about what becomes of Spirits—or spiritual beings—as they grow after death; how Forms exist in the barzakh and what kind of world is theirs; and what is meant by the worlds of paradise and hell. All of this accords with my own doctrine of being, and of its increasing and decreasing degrees of intensity.”

As we have already noted, Sadra Shirazi considers the whole question of resurrection in the light of his metaphysics of being. This reverses the traditional metaphysics of essences, which cannot, in the end, reach the very act of existing. We have seen that the intensification and weakening of this act of existing—which give being its movement, its essential restlessness—also allow us to understand its unity. That is why, when faced with two questions, “Is this one and the same world?” and “Are these two different worlds?”, Mulla Sadra answers that the first is the one to which we must say yes.

For “the relationship between the Forms that appear in the barzakh and those that exist at the Great Resurrection is simply the relationship between an incomplete and imperfect degree of being and the fullness and perfection of being. It is the same relationship as that between infancy and maturity. This is what our Prophet alludes to when he says: ‘The tomb is a garden among the gardens of paradise, or else a pit among the pits of hell.’”

Here the tomb means the tomb in its true sense: not a grave in a cemetery, but the intermediate world itself. So long as the soul remains in this “tomb,” dwelling in the intermediate world, it is like a small child in its cradle. And, characteristically for a Persian scholar, Mulla Sadra illustrates his philosophical discussion with a couplet by Ferdowsi: “We cannot escape our passage through the tomb, for the soul has no cradle but the tomb.”

What concerns us, then, is the interval between the Lesser Resurrection (Qiyâmat soghrâ), when the soul passes from the sensory world to the supersensory intermediate world, and the Greater Resurrection (Qiyâmat kobrâ), when its “resurrection body” comes to full maturity and it passes into the world of Spirit. Life in the intermediate world is the period in which the soul and the subtle body it acquired during its earthly life continue to grow. This subject will be developed at length in the last Gloss discussed below (Gloss 629). Here, in Glosses 620 and 621, Mulla Sadra considers how this subtle or “resurrection” body grows, and what kind of world allows that growth to take place.

While the soul inhabits the material body of this world, it is like an embryo in the womb. Dying to this world, it is born into another, into the barzakh, which becomes its “cradle” (we shall see below that Ibn Arabi slightly changes this imagery).

The “subtle body” that the soul takes with it on leaving this world is its imaginal body (jism mithâlî), the body it has acquired (jism moktasab) through every way it has lived, thought, and acted. It is this imaginal body that must grow to maturity. And this is why only the doctrine of an active Imagination—an imagination that has its own substantial reality and gives substance to the body the soul forms for itself—allows us to understand fully the meaning of ma'âd jismânî, or “bodily” resurrection.

Mulla Sadra is equally explicit on this point: “If we speak of resurrection in natural physical bodies, and mean dense material bodies like those of this world—that is, we might say, bodies belonging to the carbon cycle, mutable, impermanent, and perishable—then this is entirely false. It leads to such impossibilities as tanâsokh [the transmigration of souls], and to absurdities I cannot discuss here.
“But if we mean other bodies, belonging to another creation, bodies acquired by and for the soul, given bodily form (mojassam) in keeping with the soul’s deeds and ways of being—then yes.”

Once again, as we have seen, identity can be affirmed precisely because the soul, not matter, is recognized as the principle that makes an individual what he is. “Each of these bodies may be said to be the body that existed in this world, if by that we mean the unity of the soul, since it is the soul that makes the body an individual body.” Zayd’s body in paradise, for example, really is the same body he had in this world, because the same soul gives it its individuality.

What matters, and what makes identity conceivable, is not the material condition of the body but the identity of the active principle (fâ'il) that determines its matter. That principle is the Soul, which transforms the substance of its body as it undergoes its own transformation. This is entirely different from the transmigration of souls. “It is,” our philosopher says, “like lead transmuted into gold in a furnace.”

To support the view that the Spirit dwelling in the barzakh, together with the Form that accompanies it as its subtle body, stands in the relation of the imperfect to the perfect, Mulla Sadra quotes another passage from Ibn Arabi.

There the barzakh is described as “an intermediate state during which Spirits inhabit bodies of imagination (ajsâd khayâlîya), like those they inhabit in this world during sleep. … Once you have understood the individual resurrection (qiyâmat joz'îya) that takes place at each person’s death, you will also understand that the universal resurrection (qiyâmât 'âmma) follows the same pattern for each individual. The time spent in the barzakh, in relation to the Other Growth, is like the time a woman carries a child in her womb.

“God brings it forward gradually, from one stage of growth to another, until it is born on the day of the Great Resurrection. That is why it is said of one who dies that ‘his resurrection has already begun’ (idhâ mâta faqad qâmat qiyâmatoh). The Other Growth has already begun to unfold in the barzakh, until the day the person is brought forth from it, just as at birth he was brought forth from his mother’s womb onto this Earth.”

Since the intermediate world of the barzakh stands to the world after the Great Resurrection as the imperfect stands to the perfect, and since the two realms mirror one another symbolically, they must have something in common in their mode of existence. Mulla Sadra first describes this shared character as a philosopher, then evokes it through a beautiful visionary symbol.

Gloss 621 (lithographed edition, p. 512) begins by rejecting any trace of what we would now call “psychologism”—the reduction of realities to mere psychological states. For some thinkers, imaginal Forms (sowar mithâlîya) are simply attributes that exist within the imaginative faculty, just as intelligible Forms are supposedly attributes existing within the intellect. Those who hold the first position forget that subtle Forms exist independently of imagination; those who hold the second have misunderstood the unity of the intellect, what it knows, and the act of knowing.

“The truth,” Mulla Sadra writes, “is that every essence possessing substantial reality (haqâ'iq jawhârîya) exists in each of the three worlds: the sensory, the imaginal, and the intelligible. In the last two it is immaterial (mojarrada); in the sensory world it is material (mâddîya).”

There are spiritual constellations, constellations of souls, just as there are constellations in the astronomical heavens. “What we maintain,” our philosopher declares emphatically, “is that these Forms have no material substratum—whether one imagines that substratum to be a celestial faculty, such as the World Soul’s imaginative faculty, or our own individual power of imagination. For they have extension and dimensions (miqdârîya), and yet are separate from matter.

“If one says that they subsist through the immaterial faculties of the soul, the kind of subsistence meant must never be confused with inherence (holûl): the way an attribute, such as blackness, exists within its substratum (mahall), the black body that bears it. Far from it! In the world beyond, each human spiritual substance (jawâhir al-Adamîyîn) is a complete universe in its own right, as complete as the whole of this sensory world, without crowding or constraining any other such universe. Every human being in paradise is a complete universe in himself.

“And precisely because that universe is a whole, it is not merely one unit among others of the same kind, all of which would have to be added together to make a single complete universe. Although each universe is itself complete and unique, whatever its inhabitant wishes or desires—another human presence or anything else—is made present to him in the blink of an eye or a heartbeat.”
It would be hard to imagine a conception more thoroughly monadological than Mulla Sadra’s: one that recalls both Leibniz’s philosophy of monads and Swedenborg’s angelology.

We must not think of a spiritual whole as something assembled by adding up parts, each incomplete without the others. Strictly speaking, there are no parts. The whole is present in each. Unity, then, is not a universal community formed by gathering separate individuals together. Each individual contains the whole within himself; each is, in this sense, universal.

“This also explains,” Mulla Sadra says, “why God is the Lord of the worlds. Each divine universe is complete, lacking nothing, needing nothing beyond itself or beyond the bounds of its own realm and sovereignty.” There is no need here to invoke the familiar “staircase” argument against an actually infinite series, or the supposed impossibility of infinite dimensions. “Each of these universes has the vastness of the heavens and the earth, without interpenetration, crowding, or contact. No: things are just as the visionary mystics (mokâshifûn) and the angels nearest to God (moqarrabûn) understand them.”

Everything we have said about the creative Imagination as a purely psycho-spiritual faculty—the soul’s subtle covering, independent of the physical body—culminates in this vision. When the subtle organism separates from the material body, which perishes as a result, that subtle organism remains capable of sensory perceptions, but on a spiritual level, without needing material objects. For sensory perception itself already presupposes an underlying spiritual perception.

To imagine that the soul, once separated from its physical body and organs, must suffer from their loss is to misunderstand our philosophers’ theory of knowledge. For them, what we perceive through the senses is already spiritual. Freed from the physical conditions that disturb perception in this world, imaginative consciousness can at last share in divine freedom and power.
